`tree`: list directories as a tree.

## Synopsis

<strong>tree</strong> \[<strong>-a</strong>\] \[<strong>-d</strong>\] \[<strong>-L</strong> <em>level</em>\] \[<strong>--noreport</strong>\] \[<em>dir</em>...\]

## Description

<strong>tree</strong> prints each <em>dir</em> (the working directory when none is named), then its contents as a tree, drawn with lines, descending into every directory. A symbolic link is shown as <em>name</em> <strong>-\></strong> <em>target</em> and is not followed. Names starting with a dot are left out.

At the end it reports how many directories and files it showed, for all the dirs together.

## Options

<strong>-a</strong>
: Shows names starting with a dot too.

<strong>-d</strong>
: Shows directories only; the report then counts only directories.

<strong>-L</strong> <em>level</em>
: Descends at most <em>level</em> levels (1: only the directory's own entries). It must be greater than 0.

<strong>--noreport</strong>
: Leaves the report out.

<strong>-a</strong> and <strong>-d</strong> can be joined (<strong>-ad</strong>).

## Exit status

0 on success; 1 for an invalid option or level; 2 if a <em>dir</em> isn't a directory (it is shown as <em>dir</em> <strong>\[error opening dir\]</strong> and the others are still listed).

## Examples

```text
tree
tree -L 1 /
tree -d /lib
```

## See also

<strong>ls</strong>(1), <strong>find</strong>(1), <strong>du</strong>(1)
